title: The Power of the Third Turn
author: Sol in the Wild
summary: The author introduces the 'third turn' as a targeted instructional move that transforms classroom discussion from a simple question-answer-evaluate sequence into a dialogic learning experience. Every classroom discussion has three moves: the teacher's question (first turn), the student's response (second turn), and what the teacher does with that response (third turn). Most classroom talk stops at turn two; the third turn instead treats the student's answer as a starting point for a follow-up that extends, challenges, clarifies, or connects thinking—often by handing it to other students. The technique is grounded in cognitive science principles: retrieval practice, elaboration, and self-explanation all strengthen memory and understanding beyond simple recall. Four practical third-turn moves—Build, Extend, Challenge/Clarify, and Reposition—can be planned in advance with scripted follow-up prompts keyed to each lesson's content. The key planning shift is anticipating third-turn responses before the lesson rather than improvising them, which transforms the move from a spontaneous reaction into a purposeful instructional technique.
points: The third turn—what the teacher does after a student answers—is the most underused instructional move in classroom talk; it turns a correct answer into a launching point for retrieval, elaboration, and self-explanation by additional students.

Four practical third-turn prompt types—Build (add an example), Extend (connect to a concept), Challenge/Clarify (ask for evidence), and Reposition (offer another perspective)—can be scripted before the lesson to ensure they are planned rather than improvised.

Rotating the third-turn prompts across different students, rather than returning to the same voices, keeps the whole class covertly retrieving and makes the discussion a collaborative dialogue rather than a single teacher-student exchange.
quotes: One question sits behind most of my instructional decisions now: how do I get all of the students thinking more actively, frequently, and deeply about what they're learning?

Every classroom discussion, especially one led by cold call, has three moves: First turn: the teacher’s question. Second turn: the student’s response. Third turn: what the teacher does with that response.

The third turn treats the answer as a starting point of the dialogue. Instead of evaluating and moving on, the teacher uses a follow-up prompt to extend, challenge, clarify, or connect student's thinking, often by handing it to other students.
A first answer is usually only the beginning of understanding and discussion. Students may be able to recall a fact without fully articulating the concept behind it.

the third turn done well creates more opportunities for more students to rehearse their understanding, clarify each other’s thinking, connect concepts, and support their answers with evidence. Instead of the teacher simply confirming whether an answer is right or wrong, the conversation becomes a dialogic learning experience where all students are listening, processing, and making meaning.
